newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel finance ministry choice relieves investors.
newsitem.headline: Israel finance ministry choice relieves investors.

text.p: Investors breathed a sigh of relief on Monday at the naming of Israel's new finance minister -- not because of who he is but because of who he isn't.
In a surpise move designed to end a smouldering cabinet crisis, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu named former justice minister Yaacov Neeman as finance minister.

"They (investors) don't know Neeman but the fact that he's not Ariel Sharon is a good start," said Stephen Levey of Carnegie Emerging Markets in London. "The celebration may be short-lived until they find out what the guy is like."

Sharon, the hawkish national infrastructure minister, had been tipped as the leading contender for the finance post, vacant since Netanyahu's party rival Dan Meridor resigned last month in a power struggle with Netanyahu over foreign exchange policy.
Investors had feared Sharon, with a budget-busting reputation, would show less fiscal restraint than Meridor.
"Fiscal restraint is the key issue for the whole economy and the capital markets," said Victor Shohet, chief economist at Ofek Securities.

The new finance minister will face a tough battle in trying to cut the 1998 budget by the 3.5 billion shekels to 4.0 billion shekels ($985 million-$1.1 billion) analysts say is necessary to reduce inflationary pressures and revive sustainable growth.
"Neeman is a bit of an unknown quantity," Shohet said. "They (the markets) are happy on default but that's obviously a short-term reaction. Over the longer term people will start studying him."

Neeman served a brief stint as justice minister but his indictment last August on charges of obstructing justice and lying under oath forced him to leave the job Netanyahu had given him less than two months earlier. A court cleared Neeman of charges in May.
A prominent attorney, Neeman served as Treasury director-general in 1979-81 during the government of former prime minister Menachem Begin.
Yoram Gabbay, a former Treasury revenues director and now a fund manager, said Neeman was an expert in international taxes who had worked with many important foreign investors.
"On the micro level he has a good background, less so on macro. He is not an economist," said Gabbay.

Gabbay said he expects Neeman to continue on the path of economic liberalisation and budgetary restraint. But he said he doubted any finance minister would be given much room to act, given the demands of Netanyahu's fractious coalition.

Gabbay said the new finance minister may be forced to raise taxes, which would be easier for Netanyahu's coalition partners to accept than budget cuts. Shohet said the coalition appears to be very weak and members may try to buy stability by increasing spending.

"The new minister will have to very strong. He will have to get the complete backing of the prime minister because he's an outsider, he's not a politician. If not, he will be swamped by politicians," Shohet said.
The economist said he was optimistic there would be some sort of fiscal restraint as Netanyahu in the past has given strong backing to controlling government expenditures.
Analysts said the fact that Neeman was a technocrat and not a politican was a plus. Neeman's appointment is unusal in that he is not a member of parliament.
Sharon, for example, seemed more interested in using the prominent finance post to raise his profile in security matters rather than in leading the economy, they said.
"Neeman won't have much of a say in security. He will be much more dedicated to managing finance," Shohet said. "The big question is what are his views."
-Tel Aviv newsroom, 972-3-537-2211 ($ = 3.552 Israeli Shekels)
